docs: After serialising the transformed type, advance the cursor by `offset` bytes interpreted via the chosen strategy.

Since the offset is applied _after_ the transformed type runs, this transform is useful to move the cursor around once the transformed type has been processed. See `preOffsetTransformNode` for the opposite behaviour.

The strategies below are illustrated against the following buffer: the `99` byte represents the encoded value of the transformed type and the `FF` byte represents the next bytes to be encoded after it, in order to show the _post_ cursor position.
| └-- Initial post-offset
└-- Pre-offset
**`relative`** — the cursor is moved to the right by the provided offset. A negative offset moves it to the left instead.
offset = 2
└-- Post-offset
offset = -2
└-- Post-offset
**`absolute`** — the cursor is moved to an absolute position in the buffer. A negative offset moves it backwards from the end of the buffer.
offset = 0
└-- Post-offset
offset = -2
└-- Post-offset

**`padded`** — the cursor is moved to the right by the provided offset **and the buffer size is increased** by the offset amount, allowing padding bytes to be added. Reciprocally, a negative offset moves the cursor to the left and decreases the buffer size.
offset = 2
└-- Post-offset
offset = -2
0x0000FF990000; <- Size = 6 (initially 8)
└-- Post-offset

**`preOffset`** — the cursor is moved to the right of the pre-offset — i.e. where the transformed type started — by the provided offset. A negative offset moves it to the left of the pre-offset instead.
offset = 2
|   └-- Post-offset = Pre-offset + 2
└-- Pre-offset
offset = -2
|   └-- Pre-offset
└-- Post-offset = Pre-offset - 2
> [!IMPORTANT]
> Some transforms affect the buffer that is available to us: depending on where we are in the type tree, we may not have access to the entire buffer.

> For instance, under a `fixedSizeTransformNode`, the buffer is truncated or padded to match the provided fixed size once the transformed content has been serialised — we are essentially "boxed" into a sub-buffer, and that sub-buffer is the one affected by the `absolute` strategy.
> The transforms that create sub-buffers are: `fixedSizeTransformNode`, `sentinelTransformNode`, and `sizePrefixTransformNode`.

docs: The signed byte offset to apply after the transformed type runs.

attributes.name: strategy
docs: How the `offset` value is interpreted.

An absolute post-offset from the end of the buffer

docs: Before serialising the transformed type, advance the cursor by `offset` bytes interpreted via the chosen strategy.

Since the offset is applied _before_ the transformed type runs, this transform is useful to move the encoded value of the transformed type itself. See `postOffsetTransformNode` for the opposite behaviour.

The strategies below are illustrated against the following buffer: the `99` byte represents some previously encoded value for reference and the `FF` byte represents the encoded value of the transformed type, which moves as its pre-offset changes.
└-- Initial pre-offset
**`relative`** — the cursor is moved to the right by the provided offset. A negative offset moves it to the left instead.
offset = 2
└-- Pre-offset
offset = -2
└-- Pre-offset
**`absolute`** — the cursor is moved to an absolute position in the buffer. A negative offset moves it backwards from the end of the buffer.
offset = 0
└-- Pre-offset
offset = -2
└-- Pre-offset

**`padded`** — the cursor is moved to the right by the provided offset **and the buffer size is increased** by the offset amount, allowing padding bytes to be added. Reciprocally, a negative offset moves the cursor to the left and decreases the buffer size.
offset = 2
└-- Pre-offset
offset = -2
0x0000FF990000; <- Size = 6 (initially 8)
└-- Pre-offset
> [!IMPORTANT]
> Some transforms affect the buffer that is available to us: depending on where we are in the type tree, we may not have access to the entire buffer.

> For instance, under a `fixedSizeTransformNode`, the buffer is truncated or padded to match the provided fixed size once the transformed content has been serialised — we are essentially "boxed" into a sub-buffer, and that sub-buffer is the one affected by the `absolute` strategy.
> The transforms that create sub-buffers are: `fixedSizeTransformNode`, `sentinelTransformNode`, and `sizePrefixTransformNode`.

categories.name: display
docs: Display nodes — presentation metadata attached to instructions, accounts, fields, and enum variants.
Display metadata that presents a number as a scaled amount with an optional unit.
The value is divided by `10 ^ decimals` and rendered alongside `unit` (e.g. `"USDC"`, `"%"`, `"bps"`).

attributes.name: decimals
docs: How many decimal places scale the underlying integer. Resolved as a number value: either a literal `numberValueNode` or a key resolved from a surrounding provider.
A value of `1000000` with `decimals` resolving to `6` renders as `1`.
When this input cannot resolve, renderers should fall back to presenting the raw value rather than guess the scale.

attributes.name: unit
docs: A label appended after the scaled value (e.g. `"USDC"`, `"%"`, `"bps"`). Resolved as a string value: either a literal `stringValueNode` or a key resolved from a surrounding provider.
When this input cannot resolve, renderers should present the scaled value without a unit.

examples.title: A fixed 9-decimal SOL amount

content: display: amountNumberDisplayNode({ decimals: numberValueNode(9), unit: stringValueNode('SOL') }),

examples.title: Decimals and unit injected from surrounding account state

content: // 1_500_000 with injected decimals 6 and symbol "USDC" => "1.5 USDC"

docs: Display metadata that presents a number as a point in time.
The underlying value counts ticks since the Unix epoch; `ticksPerSecond` is the divisor that converts those ticks back to seconds.

attributes.name: ticksPerSecond
docs: How many ticks make one second. Defaults to `1` (the value is already in seconds).
Common choices are `1000` (milliseconds), `1000000` (microseconds), and `1000000000` (nanoseconds).

docs: Display metadata that presents a number as an elapsed duration.
The underlying value counts ticks; `ticksPerSecond` is the divisor that converts those ticks back to seconds.
Renderers typically format the result as `HH:mm:ss` or a coarser human-readable form.

attributes.name: ticksPerSecond
docs: How many ticks make one second. Defaults to `1` (the value is already in seconds).
Common choices are `1000` (milliseconds), `1000000` (microseconds), and `1000000000` (nanoseconds).

docs: Display metadata for an instruction: a short intent label and an interpolated sentence template.
Either form may be absent; presentation strategy is left to the renderer.

attributes.name: intent
docs: A short imperative label describing what the instruction does (e.g. `"Transfer"`).

attributes.name: interpolatedIntent
docs: A sentence template that composes the instruction into prose with `${root…}` placeholders.

Roots are `data` (the instruction data) and `accounts` (the instruction accounts). After the `data` root, placeholders embed the shared path-expression grammar (e.g. `${data.amount}`, `${data.config.fees[0]}`, `${data[0]}`); after the `accounts` root, exactly one account identifier follows (e.g. `${accounts.destination}`) — accounts resolve to addresses, so nothing nests.
A placeholder renders through its referent's own presentation; the `skip` rule governs the fallback list only and never the sentence.

Indices apply to the decoded character sequence.

attributes.name: sliceEnd
docs: The end index of the displayed slice, exclusive. Defaults to the end of the string.
Indices apply to the decoded character sequence.

docs: Display metadata for a named member: its label, whether it is shown in the fallback list, and whether it is flattened into its parent.
Value presentation is carried by the member's type; this node only addresses naming and composition.

attributes.name: label
docs: An override label shown for the member (e.g. `"Amount"`).
When absent, renderers derive a label from the member `name`.

attributes.name: skip
docs: Whether the member is shown in the fallback list. Defaults to `"never"` (always shown).

attributes.name: flatten
docs: When `true`, the member's type is expected to be a struct and its fields are lifted into the parent's context, dropping the field name as an extra level of nesting.
Flattening lives on the field rather than on the struct so the same struct can be flattened in one place and nested in another.
Meaningful only when the member's type is structurally a struct; renderers ignore it otherwise.

attributes.name: flattenPrefix
docs: A literal prefix prepended to each flattened member's label (e.g. `"args."`).
Meaningful only when `flatten` is `true`. Useful to disambiguate when two flattened children might collide.

enumerations.name: bytesEncoding

variants.name: base16
docs: Hexadecimal encoding (two characters per byte).

variants.name: base58
docs: Base58 encoding, the standard for Solana addresses.

variants.name: base64
docs: Base64 encoding (RFC 4648).

variants.name: utf8
docs: UTF-8 text encoding.
How a string of bytes is encoded for transport.

enumerations.name: defaultValueStrategy

variants.name: omitted
docs: The attribute is not exposed as a parameter in the generated API; the default value is always used.

variants.name: optional
docs: The attribute is exposed as an optional parameter; callers may override the default value.
How an attribute that carries a default value is exposed in generated APIs.

enumerations.name: displaySkip

variants.name: always
docs: The member is never shown in the fallback list. Use for purely structural fields like discriminators.

variants.name: never
docs: The member is always shown in the fallback list. This is the default.

variants.name: whenInjected
docs: The member is shown only when its value was not already surfaced elsewhere through the provide/inject graph.
When the value was pulled via injection, the member is hidden as redundant; when nothing surfaced it, the member appears under its label as a backup.
Whether a member should be hidden from the fallback display list.
The interpolated sentence on `instructionDisplayNode` is governed separately — a member may be referenced there regardless of its skip value.

enumerations.name: endianness

variants.name: be
docs: Big-endian: the most significant byte is written first.

variants.name: le
docs: Little-endian: the least significant byte is written first.
The byte order of a numeric serialization.

enumerations.name: instructionLifecycle

variants.name: archived
docs: No longer included in client SDKs. Retained in the IDL for historical reference only.

variants.name: deprecated
docs: Still callable but discouraged. Clients should migrate to a replacement instruction.

variants.name: draft
docs: Work-in-progress. The instruction may change before it stabilises.

variants.name: live
docs: Stable and supported for production use.
The lifecycle stage of an instruction.

enumerations.name: numberFormat

variants.name: f32
docs: IEEE-754 32-bit floating point.

variants.name: f64
docs: IEEE-754 64-bit floating point.

variants.name: i8
docs: Signed 8-bit integer.

variants.name: i16
docs: Signed 16-bit integer.

variants.name: i32
docs: Signed 32-bit integer.

variants.name: i64
docs: Signed 64-bit integer.

variants.name: i128
docs: Signed 128-bit integer.

variants.name: shortU16
docs: Solana compact-u16 encoding: a variable-length unsigned integer occupying 1 to 3 bytes. Values up to `0x7f` are stored as-is in a single byte; above that, the top bit of each byte is set and the remaining value continues in the next byte, with the third byte — when needed — using all 8 bits.

variants.name: u8
docs: Unsigned 8-bit integer.

variants.name: u16
docs: Unsigned 16-bit integer.

variants.name: u32
docs: Unsigned 32-bit integer.

variants.name: u64
docs: Unsigned 64-bit integer.

variants.name: u128
docs: Unsigned 128-bit integer.
The wire format of a numeric serialization.

enumerations.name: optionalAccountStrategy

variants.name: omitted
docs: The account slot is left out of the instruction entirely. Subsequent accounts shift up.

variants.name: programId
docs: The account slot is filled with the program ID as a placeholder, preserving positional indices.
How an absent optional account is represented when serialising an instruction.

enumerations.name: postOffsetStrategy

variants.name: absolute
docs: Move the cursor to the absolute byte position given by the offset; a negative offset counts backwards from the end of the buffer.

variants.name: padded
docs: Move the cursor like `relative` while growing the buffer by the offset amount; a negative offset moves the cursor backwards and shrinks the buffer.

variants.name: preOffset
docs: Move the cursor by the offset bytes relative to the pre-offset — where the transformed type started — rather than where it ended; a negative offset moves it to the left of that position.

variants.name: relative
docs: Advance the cursor by the offset bytes relative to its current position; a negative offset moves it backwards.
How a post-offset transform interprets its offset value after serialising the transformed type.
See `postOffsetTransformNode` for an illustrated walkthrough of each strategy.

enumerations.name: preOffsetStrategy

variants.name: absolute
docs: Move the cursor to the absolute byte position given by the offset; a negative offset counts backwards from the end of the buffer.

variants.name: padded
docs: Move the cursor like `relative` while growing the buffer by the offset amount; a negative offset moves the cursor backwards and shrinks the buffer.

variants.name: relative
docs: Advance the cursor by the offset bytes relative to its current position; a negative offset moves it backwards.
How a pre-offset transform interprets its offset value before serialising the transformed type.
See `preOffsetTransformNode` for an illustrated walkthrough of each strategy.

docs: Attaches namespaced, plugin-specific data to a node.

A plugin is uniquely identified by its `namespace`; the optional `payload` carries arbitrary, consumer-defined data that only the matching plugin knows how to interpret. Codama itself treats the payload as opaque.
Every node can carry plugins via the `plugins` base attribute.

attributes.name: namespace
docs: The unique, dot-separated namespace identifying the plugin this data belongs to (e.g. `i18n.es`).

attributes.name: payload
docs: Arbitrary, plugin-specific data. Its shape is defined by the plugin, not by Codama, and is carried through the graph verbatim.

docs: Exposes a node under a name so consumers in the surrounding scope can resolve it by that key.
Sits inside a host's `provides` list and pairs with `injectedValueNode` on the consumer side: an injection with the matching key resolves to this entry's `node`.

attributes.name: identifier
docs: The key under which the node is exposed to consumers.

attributes.name: node
docs: The exposed node. The provider is a transparent pipe — any node may be supplied; the family check happens at the injection point against the consumer's expected family.

docs: The root of a Codama IDL.
Pairs a primary program with any number of additional programs and tags the IDL with the spec version.
![Diagram](https://github.com/codama-idl/codama/assets/3642397/96c43c75-5925-4b6b-a1e0-8b8c61317cfe)

attributes.name: standard
docs: A literal marker identifying the JSON object as a Codama IDL.
This allows other communities to fork the Codama standard under a different marker.

attributes.name: version
docs: The Codama spec version this IDL conforms to.

attributes.name: program
docs: The primary program described by the IDL.

attributes.name: additionalPrograms
docs: Additional programs referenced by the primary program.

unions.name: instructionByteDeltaValue
docs: The value forms accepted by an `instructionByteDeltaNode`.

An `accountLinkNode` uses the size of the linked account; an `argumentValueNode` uses the value of the referenced instruction argument; a `numberValueNode` uses that explicit number; and a `resolverValueNode` acts as a fallback for more complex values.

unions.name: instructionRemainingAccountsValue
docs: The value forms accepted by an `instructionRemainingAccountsNode`.
An `argumentValueNode` represents the array of accounts as a new argument of the provided name; a `resolverValueNode` acts as a fallback for more complex scenarios.
